gary.text: Bought a 200-watt marine speaker and two strings of LED rope light for the cart.
Donna asked if I'd ever played pickleball. I said no and changed the subject.
Read the parade flyer at the Town Square: sign-ups close at the end of the month.

I said to Hal: “Morning, Hal. Sorry about the Buffett, just testing the speaker and it's down now. I know the lights and sound need Architectural Review sign-off before the parade, so I'm wiring it in the garage first and filing the paperwork after.”

Donna said to Gary: “Gary, that speaker has great timing, and so do you. Come hit a few balls with me at the rec center this morning. I've got a spare paddle, it's thirty minutes, and coffee's on me.”

I said to Donna: “Alright, Donna, you win. Thirty minutes and I'm holding you to the coffee, but I'm warning you, I'll be terrible at it.”
Donna headed to Rec Center.

I said to Rosa: “Rosa, you've twisted my arm, I'll be there. I'll bring a bottle of something and leave the cart talk in the garage. Now I've got to go get embarrassed at pickleball, Donna's waiting on me.”
Rosa said to Gary: “Gary, since you're headed to the courts with Donna: dinner's tonight at six, my place. Tell her for me, and go easy on the paddle, I need you in one piece to eat.”

gary: Since Linda passed, the garage is where I feel most like myself.
Hal doesn't like me much, but nobody on this street knows wiring like I do.
Gary's guilt about the speaker and the skipped permits is nagging at me, but Hal and Rosa seem to be letting it slide for now.
Donna has been surprisingly generous with her time and her spare paddle, and I think I'm starting to look forward to our Saturday doubles match.
donna: Partners make or break your ladder ranking, and mine keep moving to Ocala.
Gary has quick hands and nothing to do on weekends. He just doesn't know he wants to play yet.
Gary is surprisingly easy to talk into things, and I'm glad he showed up to the court and kept the ball in play, even if he calls himself terrible.
Rosa's dinner invitation and the doubles partnership with Gary make me feel like this town is starting to feel like a real community again.
hal: Rules exist so neighbors don't have to argue. Somebody has to keep them.
The street was quieter before the new speaker arrived.
Gary's garage wiring worries me, but I also know the rules matter, and I'm not sure how to balance loyalty with what I owe the town.
Rosa's welcome dinner invitation surprised me, and I'm hoping I can sit at her table without turning every conversation into a complaint about flamingos.
rosa: I moved here to slow down, and so far I've worked four shifts and met nobody.
These three neighbors clearly have history I don't understand yet.
Gary turned a broken disposal into a favor I can't repay, and I think he's the kind of neighbor who shows up without being asked.
Hosting dinner for Gary, Donna, and Hal feels like the right way to thank them and finally make this street feel like home.

laws.title: Cart Modifications
laws.text: Exterior golf cart modifications visible from the street require Architectural Review approval.

laws.title: Lawn Ornaments
laws.text: No more than 3 decorative ornaments may be visible from the street.

laws.title: Quiet Hours
laws.text: No amplified sound from 10 PM to 7 AM.

laws.title: Holiday Decor
laws.text: Holiday lighting is permitted from Thanksgiving through January 15.

laws.title: Court Reservations
laws.text: Pickleball courts may be reserved for a maximum of 2 hours per party.

laws.title: Parking
laws.text: No parking on the grass. Carts and cars stay on driveways or the street.

recap_pending.story: At 8:17 on a humid, hazy Tuesday morning in Sumter Oaks, Gary is at his workbench stripping wire and bench-testing a marine speaker he plans to bolt onto his golf cart. Across the way, Donna is checking her paddles and balls and packing a spare paddle for Gary's upcoming practice sessions, optimistic as ever. Hal is sitting at his kitchen table with his violation notebook, finalizing dated entries on Gary's cart modifications and Donna's flamingo count, including Gary's grudging admission that he tends to file paperwork after the fact. Meanwhile, Rosa is scanning her shift schedule at home, hunting for an evening free of per-diem duty so she can block it off for the welcome dinner.

At 9:17 on this humid, hazy Tuesday morning in Sumter Oaks, Gary is bench-testing LED rope light strings at his workbench while sketching out his wiring plan. Donna is heading down Magnolia Loop with a determined stride, and Hal is watching the street through his binoculars to keep tabs on Gary's cart modifications and count Donna's flamingos. Meanwhile, Rosa is at her kitchen counter, planning tonight's dinner menu and jotting down the groceries she'll need for four.

At 10:17 on this humid, hazy Tuesday in Sumter Oaks, Gary is focused in his garage, running wiring and fitting a speaker mount inside his golf cart while Donna, determined as ever, makes her way down Magnolia Loop to visit him.
